strengths: Well-motivated integration of self-supervised DINO features into SLAM, addressing the limitation that existing NeRF/3DGS methods focus only on photometric consistency
General framework demonstrated to work across multiple scene representations (implicit NeRF and explicit 3DGS, with diverse encodings: hash-grid, tri-planes, neural points)
Comprehensive experimental validation across three major benchmarks (Replica, ScanNet, TUM) with consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods
Thorough ablation studies demonstrating the impact of key components and the superiority of EDINO over raw DINO features
Strong qualitative results showing improved detail preservation and completeness in reconstructions
Reproducible methodology using standard benchmarks and well-specified implementation details
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: SSE primarily combines standard MLPs and softmax cross-attention (Eqs. 2-3) without exploring alternative fusion or attention mechanisms
Insufficient justification for SSE design choices: Why these specific attention operations? Why this concatenation strategy? Why two sequential modules? No ablations on architectural variants

Questionable loss function design: Equation 7 directly supervises tri-plane encodings with EDINO features without clear justification—why should geometric/appearance encodings match semantic features?
Loss weights appear arbitrary (5.0, 0.01) with no sensitivity analysis or exploration of alternatives (L2, perceptual, contrastive losses)

Modest empirical improvements in key cases undermine the added complexity: Replica NeRF shows only 2cm accuracy gain over ESLAM; PLGSLAM still outperforms on ScanNet; 3DGS shows negligible FPS improvement despite overhead
Computational overhead inadequately analyzed: DINO extraction cost not isolated; 3DGS variant shows no FPS improvement over MonoGS; implications for real-time robotics unclear
Limited theoretical understanding: Connection between self-supervised DINO and 6-DoF SLAM accuracy asserted but not rigorously analyzed; no feature visualization or analysis of what EDINO learns
Narrow experimental scope: All evaluations on indoor scenes only; generalization to outdoor, dynamic, or visually different domains unexplored; DINO trained on ImageNet—domain shift risk unexplored

Unclear technical details: Feature dimension alignment between ViT-S (384-dim) and tri-plane resolutions not specified; 3DGS per-Gaussian feature assignment vague and potentially limiting feature expressiveness
Missing design exploration: No ablations on attention mechanisms, no comparison with simpler feature fusion approaches, no analysis of failure cases or when DINO might hurt performance

strengths: Comprehensive experimental validation across three standard benchmarks (Replica, ScanNet, TUM) with extensive comparisons to state-of-the-art methods
Demonstrated broad generality by integrating the approach into multiple scene encoding methods (hash-grid, tri-planes, neural points, 3DGS)
Dual-pipeline implementation for both NeRF and 3DGS variants shows the approach spans different neural representation paradigms
Ablation studies (Table 5) clearly establish the necessity of both DINO and EDINO components for performance gains
Well-organized presentation with clear figures explaining the architecture and approach
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the work primarily adds standard feature supervision to existing SLAM pipelines. The SSE is a relatively simple composition of MLPs and attention mechanisms without architectural innovation. No comparison to alternative self-supervised features (e.g., other vision transformers)

Marginal performance improvements on most metrics: ~9-11% on Replica NeRF, <1% on Replica 3DGS rendering (39.12 vs 38.90 PSNR), and typically 1-3% on ScanNet/TUM. Unclear if differences are practically significant or within measurement noise

Insufficient justification and analysis of SSE design: no explanation for specific attention-based fusion choice (Eqs. 2-3); no comparison to simpler fusion alternatives (concatenation, gating); no principled motivation for the particular architectural arrangement

Inadequate analysis of when and why DINO helps: no investigation of which scene properties benefit from DINO; no feature visualizations showing what EDINO captures beyond raw DINO; ablations are coarse-grained and do not explain the underlying mechanism

Significant computational overhead inadequately addressed: DINO-SLAM (NeRF) uses 48.7MB vs ESLAM's 27.2MB (~79% increase) with FPS dropping 45% (4.62→2.55). DINO feature extraction cost is not discussed, and no analysis of whether online or precomputed. Trade-off between modest accuracy gains and computational cost is not justified

Lack of theoretical grounding: the relationship between features optimized for classification/segmentation and geometric SLAM objectives is assumed but not explained; no formal analysis of why self-supervised features should improve geometric reconstruction and tracking

Hyperparameter choices appear arbitrary and unexplored: loss weights differ dramatically (5.0 for NeRF encoding loss vs 0.01 for DINO loss; 1.0 for 3DGS) with no justification or sensitivity analysis. Method may be sensitive to tuning

Limited experimental scope: all evaluations on indoor RGB-D sequences; generalization to outdoor, monocular, or other modalities unclear. DINO was trained on indoor images; potential bias not discussed
Feature metric choices underexplored: L1 distance used for feature losses without justification; cosine similarity (standard for feature matching) not explored or ablated

Missing comparisons and analyses: no direct comparison to other high-level feature-based SLAM methods; no investigation of failure modes or scenarios where DINO could hurt (e.g., novel objects); no analysis of performance on challenging scenarios (dynamic objects, low-light)
Reproducibility concerns: no code release mentioned; some MLP architectures (e.g., F_ea) not fully specified; exact DINO feature extraction details (layer, resolution) not clearly stated

Overclaimed novelty in presentation: abstract claims 'more comprehensive scene representations' without defining quantitatively; introduction calls this a 'novel and general framework' despite the incremental nature (feature supervision + standard attention fusion)

strengths: Well-motivated integration of self-supervised DINO features into SLAM, addressing a genuine limitation of pixel-wise supervision-only approaches
Comprehensive experimental validation across three standard benchmarks (Replica, ScanNet, TUM) with consistent improvements, particularly strong for 3DGS tracking (1.36 cm ATE on TUM)
Demonstrated generality through successful integration with multiple base methods (Co-SLAM, ESLAM, Point-SLAM, SplaTAM, MonoGS) and scene encodings, validating the SSE design principle
Effective dual-pipeline approach showing how EDINO features supervise scene representations differently in NeRF (tri-plane) vs. 3DGS (Gaussian parameters) contexts
Practical advantage over semantic SLAM: no annotation or pre-defined category requirements while maintaining higher-level scene understanding
Thorough ablation studies (Tables 4-5) confirming that both DINO and EDINO components are necessary, and clear implementation details enabling reasonable reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: core contribution is straightforward addition of DINO supervision to existing SLAM systems; SSE uses only standard components (MLPs, softmax cross-attention) without architectural innovation

Insufficient technical specificity: feature dimensions of fd and fed not stated, MLP architectures (Fed, Feg, Fea) undefined, loss weight ratio (5.0 vs 0.01) unjustified, and DINO inference overhead per frame not discussed

Missing statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests provided; several improvements are marginal (e.g., 1.94cm vs 2.18cm accuracy on Replica), raising questions about practical significance
Limited experimental scope: evaluation restricted to indoor RGB-D scenes with no outdoor or dynamic environment testing; generalization boundaries unclear

Unexplained design choices: the use of appearance-guided attention to refine features (Eq. 3) when appearance features are derived from DINO creates potential circularity not well justified; EDINO concatenation strategy appears ad-hoc

No failure case analysis or limitations discussion: paper lacks adversarial assessment of when the method underperforms or why; no systematic study of sensitivity to hyperparameters or architectural variants
Fairness concerns in baseline comparisons: unclear whether all methods received equal hyperparameter tuning effort; some baselines obtained from authors rather than reimplemented

Presentation issues: SSE description awkwardly transitions between equations and feature formation; notation inconsistencies (τd vs τ_d; ς vs ς^i); Figure 3 architecture diagram dense and difficult to parse

strengths: Comprehensive experimental validation across three benchmarks (Replica, ScanNet, TUM) with thorough ablation studies demonstrating consistent improvements and broad applicability across 7 different scene encodings
Well-motivated approach clearly identifying the gap between DINO's semantic understanding and SLAM's geometric requirements; elegant solution via attention-based feature fusion
Strong empirical results achieving state-of-the-art or competitive performance, particularly for GS-based variant (PSNR 41.42, LPIPS 0.021 on Replica)
Practical system design with modest computational overhead for GS variant and effective plug-and-play integration with existing SLAM methods
Clear presentation with effective figures, complete implementation details, and useful computational analysis including FPS and memory footprint
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution is standard scaled dot-product attention applied to feature projections—primarily an engineering contribution combining existing components rather than introducing novel algorithmic ideas
Significant FPS overhead for NeRF variant (45% reduction: 4.62→2.55), raising practical concerns for real-time applications despite acknowledgment

Insufficient justification of design choices: why is attention optimal? No ablation on SGE architecture, comparison with alternative fusion methods, or sensitivity analysis for loss weights (5.0, 0.01)

Critical dependency on depth quality; noise evaluation limited to Gaussian perturbations rather than realistic sensor failures; significant performance degradation with modest noise (PSNR 44.65→42.38)

Incremental improvements (typically 5-15% across metrics) with mixed results on individual benchmarks: NeRF doesn't excel on accuracy/depth L1; loses to individual baselines on some TUM sequences; PLGSLAM outperforms on ScanNet

Limited scope: only clean indoor RGB-D datasets; no challenging scenarios (outdoor, dynamic objects, extreme conditions); single DINO variant (ViT-small); no comparison with other recent DINO-SLAM approaches
Lack of theoretical analysis: no visualization of learned attention patterns, unclear what geometric properties are captured, insufficient justification for L1 feature loss over alternatives
Generalization limitations: restricted to RGB-D with depth (excludes monocular/sparse systems); frozen DINOv2 not explored for fine-tuning; hyperparameters may require per-system adjustment

strengths: Comprehensive experimental validation across three datasets with 30+ method comparisons and well-designed ablation studies (Tables 1-2) demonstrating generality across diverse scene encodings
Principled two-paradigm design (NeRF and GS) with shared SGE component showing genuine applicability beyond method-specific tuning
Strong empirical results on Replica benchmark (GS: PSNR 41.42 dB, LPIPS 0.021) with clear improvements over GauS-SLAM baseline
Effective ablation isolating geoDINO contribution, showing ~2× improvement over vanilla DINO on most metrics
Robustness analysis to depth noise (Table 4) demonstrating practical consideration of input quality
Computational transparency with detailed runtime breakdown (Table 8) and memory analysis showing moderate SGE overhead
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: SGE employs standard dual-stream attention and MLPs without architectural innovation; essentially a straightforward feature fusion mechanism that is commonplace in deep learning

Marginal improvements across most benchmarks—Replica NeRF (3-6% gains), ScanNet (~7%), TUM (~3%)—often within noise margins for dense SLAM evaluation; some metrics where DINO-SLAM does not achieve best results (e.g., Point-SLAM outperforms on Accuracy)

Significant efficiency degradation: NeRF variant 45% slower (2.55 vs 4.62 FPS); neither variant achieves real-time performance required for robotics applications, making speed-accuracy tradeoff unfavorable
Weak architectural justification: dual-pass attention (Eq. 2-3), loss function choices (L1), and concatenation strategy not ablated; design appears ad-hoc without principled alternatives explored

Incomplete technical analysis: no visualization of learned geoDINO features or attention patterns; unclear what geometric structures SGE actually captures; simple depth concatenation baseline (B') superficially addressed
Inherent limitation to RGB-D systems with significant sensitivity to depth noise (PSNR drops 2.3 dB with σ=0.1 noise); no systematic analysis across sensor modalities or noise regimes
Presentation clarity issues: limited intuitive explanation of why depth-aware attention helps SLAM; dense exposition without actionable insights into what geoDINO learns semantically

Reproducibility concerns: no explicit code availability commitment, arbitrary hyperparameter choices (k=4 keyframes, loss weights 5.0/0.01) lack sensitivity analysis, some baselines obtained from prior papers rather than re-implemented

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation identifying complementary weaknesses of semantic features (DINO) and geometric SLAM systems
Comprehensive experimental validation across 7 different scene encodings and 3 major datasets with thorough ablation studies demonstrating necessity of geoDINO over vanilla DINO features
Consistent improvements across nearly all baselines and metrics, indicating broad applicability; achieves state-of-the-art results on GS-based SLAM methods (PSNR 41.42 on Replica)
Dual NeRF and GS pipeline implementations with appropriate adaptations demonstrate thoughtful engineering and generality of approach
Strong reproducibility with detailed implementation details, computational breakdown, and ablation studies; robustness testing on depth noise shows practical applicability
Clear presentation with good motivation, well-structured content, and informative figures that effectively communicate the contribution
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: DINO features in SLAM and vanilla attention-based fusion are incremental; SGE uses standard MLPs and attention mechanisms without exploring alternative fusion strategies or providing design justifications

Insufficient justification for design choices: L1 loss selection lacks comparison with alternatives; loss weights (5.0, 0.01) have no ablation; dual-attention mechanism (Eqs. 2-3) appears arbitrary without exploration of alternatives

Significant computational overhead not adequately addressed: FPS halved for NeRF pipeline (2.55 vs 4.62 ESLAM), memory nearly doubled (48.7 vs 27.2 MB); limited mitigation strategies for real-time applications

Depth dependency limitation: method requires quality RGB-D input; robustness evaluation minimal (single scene, Gaussian noise only); no analysis of missing depth, dynamic artifacts, or large-scale scene performance

Marginal improvements on several key metrics: Replica NeRF accuracy (1.88 vs 1.94), ScanNet average tracking (6.9 vs 6.8 cm); many improvements in 0.1-0.5 unit ranges lack statistical significance testing

Missing feature analysis: no visualization of learned geoDINO features; lacks interpretability on what specific geometric properties are captured or how attention mechanisms evolve; no analysis of which loss terms contribute most to improvements

Limited evaluation scope: only clean indoor RGB-D datasets; no outdoor, dynamic, or challenging lighting scenarios; incomplete comparisons with recent semantic SLAM methods and methods using ground-truth semantic information (e.g., SNI-SLAM with masks)
